newsitem.title: UK: Sleaze issue takes centre stage in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze issue takes centre stage in UK election.

text.p: Sleaze, the issue that has dominated Britain's election campaign, takes centre stage on Tuesday when Conservatives in a party stronghold decide the fate of a candidate embroiled in an influence-peddling row.
MP Neil Hamilton has so far stood firm against calls from opposition parties and some local Conservatives to resign.
But now he must convince his local party that he can hold the northern England seat of Tatton against veteran war correspondent Martin Bell, who is standing as an independent "anti-sleaze" candidate.
Hamilton denies the allegations of corruption but opinion polls show he could be in danger of losing Tatton, the ruling Conservatives' fifth safest seat.

Bell's intervention in the May 1 election race is unprecedented in a British political system dominated by two parties. Only in recent years have single-issue candidates entered the scene and none have been as potentially pivotal as the widely-respected Bell.
The BBC correspondent has pledged to stand down if Hamilton drops out of the election campaign and says he hopes his own political career will be the shortest in history.
Highlighting his disgust with alleged shady dealings in the ruling party, Bell has offered journalists a close look at his bank accounts and tax returns.
"I have never even had my expenses queried until last November when my taxi driver in Delhi was illiterate and I didn't get a receipt. The BBC queried that," he said.

With only three weeks left until polling day, Prime Minister John Major is beginning to show his exasperation at the sleaze allegations that have dogged his party since 1993, when he launched a "back-to-basics" moral crusade.

The crusade backfired cruelly. Some 20 Conservative members of parliament have resigned since then over their involvement in sexual and financial scandals. Three have stood down since March 17 when Major set the date of the May 1 election.
"I spent the whole press conference on Monday dealing with this issue," a clearly-rattled Major said on Tuesday.
"I am not having the whole of this general election campaign being hijacked by one constituency."
The Conservatives, trailing Labour by more than 20 points in opinion polls, have struggled to turn the campaign spotlight onto flaws in the opposition Labour Party's manifesto.
Hamilton, a former industry ministry, made clear once more that he would not help the prime minister by standing down.
"My husband is not a quitter. We will not be backing down now," Hamilton's wife Christine told reporters on Tuesday. "It is appeasement if you do that. It is not the spirit that won the war."
In fact, Bell's intervention appeared to have rallied local Conservatives around their candidate. The party will decide on his fate at a meeting at a pub on Tuesday evening.
Many local people regard Bell as an interloper from faraway London who has been foisted on Tatton by trendy media types.
Tony Martin, Conservative Association treasurer in the Tatton constituency who had been fighting to oust Hamilton, said Bell "has probably torpedoed my campaign."
